title: Explainable churn prediction in telecom with tabular ML five model benchmark and SHAP analysis
venue: Discover Artificial Intelligence (Springer Nature; Crossref publisher string 'Springer Science and Business Media LLC'; eISSN 2731-0809)
harvard_reference: Zerine, I., Islam, M.M., Khan, M.A.U., Chy, M.A.R., Saimon, A.S.M., Manik, M.M.T.G. and Wata, C. (2026) 'Explainable churn prediction in telecom with tabular ML five model benchmark and SHAP analysis', Discover Artificial Intelligence, 6(1), 263. doi:10.1007/s44163-026-00983-0.
abstract_summary: Benchmarks five tabular learners (elastic-net logistic regression, RBF SVC, random forest, XGBoost, and a small MLP) on a Kaggle Telco Customer Churn snapshot using nested cross-validation (5 stratified outer folds, 3 inner folds; PR-AUC as the tuning objective; F1-optimal threshold chosen on inner validation). The MLP is reported best on every metric (accuracy 0.92, precision 0.88, recall 0.82, F1 0.85, ROC-AUC 0.95, PR-AUC 0.82); XGBoost is the best classical baseline (accuracy 0.89, F1 0.69, ROC-AUC 0.91), random forest 'followed closely', logistic regression had lower recall (F1 0.64) and SVC was weakest (F1 0.59). Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests across the five folds are at trend level two-sided (p = 0.0625-0.1875) and significant one-sided only against LR and SVC. SHAP, PDP and ICE show churn risk falling monotonically with tenure with a tipping point near three years, rising steeply from zero to about five technical tickets then saturating, and amplified by high monthly charges, month-to-month contracts and fibre-optic service. Recommended interventions: contract migration, rapid ticket resolution, and targeted credits for early-life, high-charge customers.

claims_supported.claim: Tree ensembles (random forest / gradient boosting) achieve top or near-top ROC-AUC on telecom churn data, often close to logistic regression.
claims_supported.where: Section 4 (Results) and Section 5 (Conclusion). The paper reports the compact MLP as the top model on ROC-AUC (0.95 +/- 0.01) and XGBoost as the best NON-neural baseline (ROC-AUC 0.91 +/- 0.01), i.e. the MLP 'improved ... ROC AUC by 4 points' over XGBoost; random forest 'followed closely' behind XGBoost (accuracy 0.87, F1 0.66). Logistic regression's ROC-AUC is not stated in the text (Table 3 is only an image link); LR is described as the 'lower bound for performance' with F1 0.64 and recall 0.58 versus XGBoost F1 0.69. So this paper supports only the narrower point that tree ensembles were the strongest classical baselines; it contradicts the framing that tree ensembles achieve the top ROC-AUC, and gives no evidence that they are close to logistic regression. Cite it as a counter-example to the 'tree ensembles win on tabular churn' consensus, with the caveats noted.

claims_supported.claim: Explainability (SHAP or similar) identifies contract type, tenure and monthly charges (or equivalent) as key churn drivers.
claims_supported.where: Section 4.3 (Fig. 4 global SHAP beeswarm): 'Contract type, Monthly Charges, and Tenure are the dominant global drivers, with month-to-month contracts, higher charges, and shorter tenure increasing churn risk'; Section 4.4 repeats that the beeswarm 'identifies contract type, Monthly Charges, and tenure as the dominant global drivers'. Also supported by the abstract (tenure tipping point near three years; risk 'amplified by higher monthly charges and month to month contracts with fiber users most sensitive') and Section 4.3 SHAP dependence/PDP/ICE for tenure and technical tickets.

claims_supported.claim: Business or profit-oriented evaluation changes which model or threshold is preferred compared with accuracy-only evaluation.
claims_supported.where: Not demonstrated. Model selection and thresholding are statistical, not profit-based: the tuning objective is PR-AUC (Section 3.4) and 'the decision threshold is chosen on the inner validation data to maximize the F1 score' (Sections 3.4, 3.5). Section 4.5 states 'While this study reports threshold-independent metrics, the predicted probabilities enable cost-based threshold selection by minimizing expected misclassification cost or maximizing expected monetary value (EMV)' and Section 4.4 recommends sequencing outreach by 'expected business value, defined as the product of predicted churn probability and customer value net of treatment cost' - but no profit/EMV evaluation is actually run and no change in model or threshold preference is shown. The Conclusion explicitly lists 'cost sensitive learning and explicit thresholding tied to treatment budgets' as future work. The paper can be cited for the argument that cost-sensitive thresholding is needed, not for evidence that it changes the preferred model.

claims_supported.claim: Other specific findings useful for critical discussion: (a) imbalance handled by class weighting and XGBoost scale_pos_weight rather than SMOTE; (b) probabilities calibrated with Platt/isotonic when it improves PR-AUC, MLP Brier score 0.11 +/- 0.01; (c) the Wilcoxon tests use only five paired folds, so the smallest attainable two-sided exact p is 0.0625 - the 'significance' rests on one-sided tests (p = 0.03125 vs LR and SVC; RF p = 0.0625 and XGBoost p = 0.09375 remain non-significant); (d) tenure tipping point 'near the late third year', technical-ticket risk rising from 0 to ~5 tickets then saturating, fibre subscribers most sensitive; (e) authors state SHAP 'explains associations, not causes', results come from a single public dataset, and uplift, survival (time-to-churn), causal what-if, drift monitoring and fairness auditing are deferred to future work.
claims_supported.where: (a) Section 3.5: 'Class imbalance is addressed with class weighting for learners that support it and with a positive class scaling term for boosting'; (b) Section 3.5 and Section 4.5 ('mean Brier score of 0.11 +/- 0.01'); (c) Section 4.1: 'Exact p-values were computed because there are five paired observations per comparison', W = 0.0, two-sided p = 0.0625 vs LR and SVC; RF W = 1.0, p = 0.1250; XGBoost W = 2.0, p = 0.1875; one-sided p = 0.03125, 0.0625, 0.09375; (d) Sections 4.3 and 4.4; (e) Section 4.6 (Limitations) and Section 5 (Conclusion, final sentence).

caveats: (1) Internal inconsistencies the student should note if citing the numbers: the abstract gives a class ratio of 'approximately two point seven seven to one' but Section 3.1 gives 28%/72% = 'about two point five seven to one'; Sections 3.1-3.2 describe an 'expanded snapshot' of 8,093 customers and 34 input features including technical-ticket counts, whereas the Data Availability statement points to the standard Kaggle blastchar dataset (7,043 rows, 21 columns, no ticket fields). Ticket-count features exist only in the IBM Cognos 'Telco customer churn (11.1.3+)' variant, where numTechTickets is known to be extremely predictive; this likely explains the reported 92% accuracy / 0.95 ROC-AUC, which are far above the ~80-82% accuracy and ~0.84-0.86 ROC-AUC typically reported on the standard 7,043-row dataset. Results are therefore NOT directly comparable with studies on the standard Kaggle dataset. (2) Tables 3-6 are not in the HTML text (image/link only), so per-model ROC-AUC for LR, RF and SVC could not be read; only MLP (0.95) and XGBoost (0.91) are quoted in prose. (3) The statistical testing is under-powered by construction (n = 5 folds); the authors themselves describe two-sided results as 'trend level'. (4) The reproduction pack is described but no repository URL appears in the text. (5) Section 4.5 is mis-headed as a second 'Business implications' section (it actually covers robustness, calibration and fairness checks). (6) The 'Scout' lead listed six models; the paper benchmarks five - 'Logistic Regression with Elastic Net' is one model, not two.
